---

# What I'd do differently starting a mentorship program

Our first version was a spreadsheet. Two columns, mentors and mentees, paired by whoever had overlapping calendars. It lasted nine weeks.

The problem wasn't the matching. It was that nobody knew what the meetings were for. A senior engineer would block 30 minutes, ask "so, how's it going?", and get "fine." Both people left feeling like they'd wasted half an hour, because they had.

The second version worked, mostly because we made it narrower. Each pair picks one thing to work on for a quarter — get comfortable reviewing code outside your own service, run an incident, write a design doc that survives contact with the staff engineers. One goal, written down somewhere the manager can see it.

We also stopped calling it mentorship for career growth. That framing pulled every conversation toward promotion, which is a conversation for a manager, not a mentor. The mentor's job is smaller than that: help this person get good at one specific thing, and tell them when the work isn't there yet.

Two things I'd guard hard. Mentors need cover — an hour a week that doesn't come out of their sprint, or the program becomes the first thing to slip when a release gets tight. And let pairs end. We check in at week six and either side can walk with no explanation. Three pairs did that in the first cycle, which I count as the program working. A bad match that limps along for six months teaches a junior engineer that asking for help is a chore for everybody.

Start with four pairs. Not the whole team.

---

The concrete numbers — nine weeks, week-six check-in, three pairs, four to start — are invented to give the piece texture. Swap in yours before publishing, or tell me the real ones and I'll rework it around them.
